Secure Browser FAQs
This topic answers common questions about Secure Browser.
-
What is the CyberArk Secure Browser?
.CyberArk Secure Browser is an enterprise-focused web browser designed with a security-first approach that provides security, privacy, and productivity for accessing web-based resources while delivering a seamless user experience. With CyberArk Secure Browser, customers gain visibility into end-user activity, enforce access controls at the browser level, and prevent attacks that leverage security gaps in consumer-focused web browsers.
CyberArk Secure Browser is designed for companies of any size that use web browsers to access high-value resources, apps, and sensitive data such as financial records, customer information, and intellectual property. With CyberArk Secure Browser, these companies can enforce access controls directly in the browser, audit in-app user activities without relying on extensive app customizations, prevent attacks that leverage cookies, and more. CyberArk Secure Browser is a perfect offering for organizations of any size to get started on an Identity Security journey. It is also a good fit for customers that need to secure remote or third-party access to resources from unmanaged and external-user devices.
-
Does Secure Browser support quick access to PAM - Self-Hosted or only Privilege Cloud?
Secure Browser protections like RDP session hijacking prevention, password replacement, cookie protections, and secure browsing are available and supported across all of CyberArk offerings (Privilege Cloud, PAM - Self-Hosted, Secure Cloud Access, Identity SSO and WPM web-apps, and the Secure Access Space).
Secure Browser sidebar provides quick-access to Identity SSO and WPM web-apps and also supports infrastructure targets for Privilege Cloud customers on the ISPSS platform. Support for additional quick access like newer Secure Access to infrastructure or self-hosted vault customers are items planned for future releases.
-
How does the Secure Browser look and feel to end users?
The Secure Browser user is built on Chromium, an open-source web browser created and maintained by Google. Other consumer browsers such as Chrome, Opera, Edge are also Chromium-based browsers. Because of this, most users will be familiar with the look and feel of Secure Browser and it will be easy for end-users to adopt and operate.
-
Since it is based on the Chromium browser, will Secure Browser still use the native Chrome password manager?
No. The Chrome password manager will be disabled inside the Secure Browser. Secure Browser will leverage CyberArk’s Workforce Password Manager natively to securely store and manage user credentials. To leverage these capabilities, customers must have a WPM license. CSB will allow customers to control the extensions allowed and blocked within the browser, so they could leverage a third-party password manager. If a customer choses to do this, they will not be able to leverage the password replacement feature. The password replacement feature works with WPM to substitute a secure and time-bound one-time passcode for the plain-text password at the time of login, keeping it from being exposed to the end-user.
-
Is Secure Browser available on Windows and Mac?
Yes. For details, see System requirements.
-
Is Secure Browser available on mobile devices?
We don’t have a defined timeline for Secure Browser on mobile at this time. But we are gathering use cases and requirements. We encourage you to open an enhancement request or speak with CyberArk Support.
-
Will the Secure Browser also be available in the Microsoft Store? Accessible via SCCM?
The only way to obtain the Secure Browser software and license is from the CyberArk platform. Customers will not be able to download it from a third-party app store. Once customers obtain the software, they will be able to distribute the software via regular solutions such as SCCM and configure manual or automatic updates as desired. For more information, see Install Secure Browser.
-
Is SWS dependent on Secure Browser?
No. SWS is a standalone product. A number of Secure Browser’s administration capabilities are built on top of SWS, but they remain separate offerings and feature sets. If the customer also has a SWS license in addition to a Secure Browser license, then all SWS capabilities should work within Secure Browser at the same or enhanced levels of functionality. In other words, Secure Browser provides another way to deliver key SWS features like session monitoring and recording, continuous authentication and more, but expands that use case further to now offer the ability to cover unmanaged devices alongside SWS’s other capabilities.
-
Does Secure Browser require admin privileges on the endpoint?
No it does not. Secure Browser can, and by default is, installed with user-level privileges on the endpoint. In addition to the security benefits and alignment with least privilege, installation in user-mode also means that it is easier for users to handle the installation themselves without requiring additional IT overhead.
-
Is the clear-text password replacement integration isolated to provide passwords from CyberArk Vault or does it also include Workforce Password Manager (WPM) passwords?
Secure Browser password replacement will cover WPM accounts where ‘prevent user from viewing the password’ checkbox is checked.
-
Is the clear-text password replacement integration isolated to only provide passwords to Secure Browser sessions?
Secure Browser password replacement protection includes an allowlist feature for validating that the intended target is meant to get the privileged password. This includes web apps within Secure Browser as well as local desktop thin or thick clients. Protection is not extended into other browsers.
-
What is meant by local storage? What kind of data is stored?
Browser local storage can be used by any web app to store small amounts of data between sessions. Each web app decides whatever it wants to store here, some simple examples might include user preferences (e.g. dark mode), session info (e.g. shopping cart info), settings (e.g. language or notification settings). And it sticks around even after you close your browser to enhance your experience the next time you visit the same web app. The risk? Some apps could also save risky values here, it might be PII like logged in username, email, or phone number, and it could also be parameters affect the security of the web-app itself - like whether some fields should be accessible to the end-user or hidden. This local storage data is easily accessed via the developer tool console available in all retail browsers – but which is inherently blocked via Secure Browser. In the future, Secure Browser will encrypt the data inside of the local storage ‘bucket’ to further protect this info from ‘prying eyes’ or issues of compliance.
-
Will Secure Browser work with the identity verification process or APIs? To limit employee access to passwords and OTPs?
Secure Browser utilizes CyberArk Identity tenant authentication. It also supports federated/chained external IdP authentication to the same CyberArk Identity tenant.
-
What is the compatibility of the browser to certain SaaS apps, plugins, incognito, etc.?
Existing investments with tools on the browser should work but were not fully tested. We will do this on a case-by-case basis.
-
Is the browser fully isolated from the underlying device and operating system?
Secure Browser is hardened against intrusion and tampering from the underlying client OS, and against being used for malicious purposes against the underlying client OS.
Optional use alongside Endpoint Privilege Manager adds process isolation, safeguards against unintended browser launches, and performs additional component verifications. It can also be used to ensure the browser accesses only what is required from the client machine, further maintaining system integrity. This comprehensive protection can be enforced during the verification page to allow access to company resources.
-
What is the difference between having a secure browser vs. having jamf/intune/ws1 manage my browser remotely?
Secure Browser supports built-in chromium policies allowing easy one-click mirroring of your existing browser protections and company configurations.
CyberArk has enhanced the browser with additional protections on top of the standard browser offering. A non-exhaustive list of the additional protections provided include enhanced protection against cookie hijacking, malicious extensions and URLs, protection for corporate web-apps, access enforcement only from Secure Browser, protections for client data on managed and unmanaged devices, data exfiltration protections, secure access to privileged apps (even with user password and vaulted credentials), RDP session hijacking protections, and more.
Secure Browser also includes operational and user-experience improvements from CyberArk by providing access to privileged apps via a native browser, without exposing the privileged account credentials and improving the security and efficiency of CyberArk RDP files. Users are also able to quickly launch their assigned protected targets via the Secure Browser sidebar for easy access to web-apps and infrastructure targets.
In addition, Secure Browser customers can seamlessly benefit from the added benefits of other CyberArk services – built-into Secure Browser.
Optional use alongside Secure Web Sessions adds recording and auditing of web-applications, MFA anywhere, download and clipboard controls, as well as protection of custom risky actions within web-applications. Secure Browser expands SWS coverage offering enforcement on unmanaged devices now as well.
Optional use alongside Workforce Password Management adds a service for securely storing, managing, and sharing business application credentials in a centralized cloud or vault. WPM is able to store data from business applications, including website URLs, usernames, passwords, and also notes like serial numbers, licenses, PINs, or other secrets. It addresses challenges like insecure password storage methods, poor visibility and control, increased complexity, and inconsistent user experience. The solution also includes features like the CyberArk Identity Browser Extension, which helps generate complex passwords and saves them in the cloud or Vault.
Optional use alongside Endpoint Privilege Manager adds process isolation, safeguards against unintended browser launches, performs additional component verifications. It can also be used to ensuring the browser accesses only what is required from the client machine, further maintaining system integrity.
-
How will the Secure Browser be distributed to endpoints?
-
Existing enterprise deployment software (SCCM, McAfee ePO, Jamf, etc.) For more information, see Install Secure Browser.
-
The page seen by users of other browsers attempting to access app meant to be reachable only via Secure Browser includes a tenant specific download link for them to use. (Can be installed in user-mode without admin rights). For more information, see Install and update Secure Browser.
-
-
How will a contractor download/install the browser if it is not pushed using any tools to their personal endpoint and the browser is not available to the public?
Secure Browser can be sent with a customer specific link for the user to download and install. No admin privileges required. Alternatively, when the user access is being verified, the user can be presented with a screen stopping them from accessing an application without Secure Browser - and your specific download link there as well. For more information, see Install and update Secure Browser.
-
Can Secure Browser provide step-up authentication for all apps? (Including non-SSO web apps)
MFA can be prompted upon specific app launch, customer's sso timeout, and optional breach of footstep tracking threshold breach. MFA anywhere applied to custom actions within any web-app can be applied via Secure Web Sessions.
-
Can a validated user who is meant to use the Secure Browser for one app open a new tab and browse elsewhere?
Secure Browser can be configured to allow open or restricted web access according to your desired policy. This can restrict access to only the intended apps and URLs, or leave the browser open for general browsing. The browser can be set to warn the user and audit any attempts to access non-approved URLs without blocking them outright.
-
How does the Secure Browser ensure enforcement, and is it secure, or could it be bypassed by something like changing the user-agent?
Secure Browser enforcement is not based on the user-agent, as that method is unreliable and easily spoofed (there are even browser extensions that allow users to change their user-agent). Instead, a proprietary method is used for Secure Browser enforcement, which differs from the signal used for SWS enforcement.
When a user accesses the verification page via Secure Browser, a session-specific secret is validated using this proprietary method. Once the verification is successfully completed by the SaaS, the rest of the configuration is securely sent and applied.
-
How does Secure Browser protect against malicious links or malware that could cause harm during an elevated session?
From the Secure Browser side, customers can enable an allowlist to restrict access to only approved and safe websites, which helps prevent accidental exposure to harmful links. Additionally, industry best practices for browser security, like CIS Benchmarks and US DoD STIG policies, can be applied or customized through the Secure Browser admin portal. These practices include managing extensions and other recommended security measures.
For customers using EPM, we've integrated with it to create special policies that add extra layers of protection for Secure Browser. These policies can isolate processes, prevent unintended browser launches, verify components, and ensure the browser only accesses what's necessary, keeping the system secure. For more details on EPM integration, see Integrate Secure Browser with Endpoint Privilege Manager.
-
Can you prevent anyone from going to GitHub from any other browser?
If an application is configured for SAML, you can mandate going through Secure Browser. You can do this directly if CyberArk Identity is the IDP, or Secure Browser can be in the middle if you have another IdP.
-
Can a 3rd party vendor access the web application with username & password type in Secure Browser from Remote Access?
Remote Access integration is on the roadmap.
-
How is the post-quantum protection leveraged in Secure Browser?
Secure Browser supports post-quantum encryption policies like, PostQuantumKeyAgreementEnabled – supporting post-quantum whenever the destination website does as well. In addition, all traffic related to Secure Browser policies and management are expected to support post-quantum encryption by the end of 2025. This is inline with AWS IOT service supporting the same. In the future, we plan to add additional post-quantum protections to further harden and protect Secure Browser customers.
-
Is it possible to swap out some libraries locally on the browser to bypass some of the controls?
Secure Browser will load only permitted component dll’s that are properly signed. This is true for both the chromium base and all additional CyberArk development. In addition, we also have built bespoke policies for Endpoint Privilege Manager which fully close this attack vector. When used together, Secure Browser can be configured to verify and enforce access only from devices with these protection policies enabled, preventing access from any exposed device. Lastly, CyberArk extensions included with Secure Browser (Secure Web Sessions, and the Identity Browser Extension), are baked into the build of the browser itself. As a result, all files and data related to these extensions are also protected from modification.
-
Can we restrict the Secure Browser unauthorized distribution from vendor end, essentially linking with the vendor machine or any secure code-based installation?
Yes, the auto-update capability of the secure browser is available. For more information, see Install Secure Browser and Install and update Secure Browser.
-
What anti-tampering protections does Secure Browser have?
Secure Browser actively verifies critical files at launch and continuously during runtime. If it detects signs of corruption, tampering, or unauthorized modification, it immediately triggers an alert and shuts down to prevent further use until it is reinstalled.

Permissions for AWS services in key policies
Many AWS services use AWS KMS keys to protect the resources they manage. When a service uses AWS owned keys or AWS managed keys, the service establishes and maintains the key policies for these KMS keys.
However, when you use a customer managed key with an AWS service, you set and maintain the key policy. That key policy must allow the service the minimum permissions that it requires to protect the resource on your behalf. We recommend that you follow the principle of least privilege: give the service only the permissions that it requires. You can do this effectively by learning which permissions the service needs and using AWS global condition keys and AWS KMS condition keys to refine the permissions.
To find the permissions that the service requires on a customer managed key, see the encryption documentation for the service. The following list includes links to some services documentation:
-
AWS CloudTrail permissions - Configure AWS KMS key policies for CloudTrail
-
Amazon Elastic Block Store permissions - Amazon EC2 User Guide and Amazon EC2 User Guide
-
AWS Lambda permissions - Data encryption at rest for Lambda
-
Amazon Q permissions - Data encryption for Amazon Q
-
Amazon Relational Database Service permissions - AWS KMS key management
-
AWS Secrets Manager permissions - Authorizing use of the KMS key

Secure native access to web applications with vaulted credentials uses a browser extension that injects the authentication credentials into the browser. This means the credentials reach the end user's workstation. To reduce the likelihood of password exposure to the end user, we recommend applying guidelines described in this section.
For the highest level of protection, use the CyberArk Secure Browser in conjunction with CyberArk Endpoint Privilege Manager (EPM). These products work together to protect both the endpoint and browser process.
If Secure Browser and EPM are not deployed, apply the following minimum hardening controls to secure your environment.
Secure the endpoint

Print functionality. For more information, see Set Chrome policies for users or browsers or Disable Printing in Microsoft Edge.

MFA caching - Linux
If this feature is enabled, by connecting to a Linux target using MFA caching, you can enter your MFA details just once and then, in a configurable time period, connect to multiple targets with minimal input.
This feature includes the following steps:
-
Get a key. To generate and download an MFA SSH key (token), use one of the following:
-
Run an SFTP command to get the SSH key.
-
Alternatively, download the key from the Secure Access space.
-
-
Use the key to connect to a target via SIA.
Step 1: Get a key
Do one of the following:
-
Run an SFTP command
-
Open an SFTP client.
-
Type the SFTP command using the following syntax:
sftp <username>@<login_suffix>#<subdomain>@key|key_ppk@<SSH gateway>:/key <key_path_on_end_user_machine>
For example:
sftp jane.doe@acme.com#acme@key@acme.ssh.cyberark.cloud:/key ~/.ssh/tenantName_janedoe
For information about the parameters, see Login command parameters.
-
-
Download from the Secure Access space
-
Go to the Secure Access space > Infrastructure.
-
Select any SSH target and click More options (...) on the right of the row. Then, click Open SSH connection guide.
-
On the connection guide, select the Token tab and then expand Authentication Token.
-
Select one of the following from the Key token format drop-down list:
-
OpenSSH: To generate a connection command in OpenSSH format.
-
PPK: To generate a connection command in Putty Private Key (PPK) format.
-
-
Click Download token or Copy SFTP command.
-
The download token functionality is replicated by the MFA key retrieval API.
-
When you use the downloaded token to connect to a target, SIA validates the IP address of the connecting machine is the same as the machine that downloaded the token. For more information, see Client IP enforcement for MFA caching.
-
The ability to download the token directly from the Secure Access space is available to users with access to the Secure Access space version of October 8, 2024 and later. Customers with earlier versions will be upgraded by arrangement. For details, contact your CyberArk representative.
-
-
Step 2: Use the key to connect to a target
Once the key has been generated, you can use it to connect to the SSH target. Use the following syntax:
ssh -i <key_path_on_end_user_machine> <username>@<login_suffix>#<subdomain>@<target>[:target_port]#<NetworkName>@<SSH gateway>
For example:
ssh -i ~/.ssh/tenantName_janedoe jane.doe@acme.com#acme@i-0d11333d451d5e4db@acme.ssh.cyberark.cloud
You can also use this key for file transfer sessions using SFTP or SCP.
For information about the parameters, see Login command parameters.

Privileged Risky Activity detection
This topic describes Privileged Risky Activity detection.
Overview
Privileged Risky Activity detection enables you to detect suspicious commands in your environment during live and recorded sessions. Privileged Detection comes with a set of default Privileged Risky Activity rules that are based on analysis performed by CyberArk Labs, and represents best practices.
In Privileged Risky Activity rules, you assign risk levels, which enable you to immediately identify and respond to the most critical threats to the organization.
Based on these rules, user activity is analyzed and events are created enabling you to get more details about suspicious command activity.
When a Privileged Risky Activity event is detected, you can configure ISI to automatically remediate the event based on the type of remediation selected in the Privileged Risky Activity rule: No action, Suspend, or Terminate.
For more information, see View and analyze Privileged Risky Activity events.
We encourage you to add Privileged Risky Activity rules or edit the default rules to best match your specific needs and policy. For more information about how to view the rules and change a rule's properties, see Manage Privileged Risky Activity rules.

Page Summary
-
App Check protects your apps from abuse by ensuring only authorized apps can acquire access and ID tokens from Google's authentication endpoints.
-
App Check uses Apple's App Attest service to verify that requests originate from your authentic app.
-
When App Check enforcement is enabled, requests from clients without a valid attestation or from unauthorized apps are rejected.
-
App Check works by having your app obtain an attestation, sending it to an App Check server for verification to receive a token, and then sending the token with requests to Google's authentication endpoints.
App Check helps protect your apps from abuse by preventing unauthorized clients from authenticating using Google Sign-in: only the apps you've authorized can acquire access tokens and ID tokens from Google's OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect endpoint.
With App Check, devices running your app use Apple's App Attest service to verify that OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect requests originate from your authentic app. This attestation is sent with every request your app makes to Google's authentication endpoints. When you enable App Check enforcement, requests from clients without a valid attestation will be rejected, as will any request originating from an app you haven't authorized.
Ready to get started?
How does it work?
When you enable App Check for Google Sign-in, the following happens whenever you access a Google OAuth 2.0 endpoint:
- Your app interacts with Apple's services to obtain an attestation of the app's authenticity.
- The attestation is sent to the App Check server, which verifies the validity of the attestation using parameters registered with the app, and returns to your app an App Check token. This token might retain some information about the attestation material it verified.
- The App Check client library sends the token along with the request to Google's authentication endpoints.
When App Check enforcement is enabled, Google only accepts requests accompanied by a current, valid App Check token.
How strong is the security provided by App Check?
App Check relies on the strength of Apple's App Attest service to determine app authenticity. It prevents some, but not all, abuse vectors directed towards your project. Using App Check does not guarantee the elimination of all abuse, but by integrating with App Check, you are taking an important step towards abuse protection for your app.

Audit
This topic describes how a CRDR incident impacts Audit functionality.
DR mode
When a CRDR incident occurs, CyberArk's SRE team will activate DR mode, moving the tenant to the DR region.
When in DR mode:
-
A banner at the top of the page indicates that DR mode is active.
-
Because services have limited functionality, Audit data is captured only for the functionality that is available in these services. See Privilege Cloud and Identity Administration disaster recovery for more information.
-
You can view and search only the Audit data stored in the DR region.
Audit limitations during DR mode
- The Activities reports page is unavailable.
-
Audit activity generated before the DR incident is unavailable during DR mode.
-
Because the DR region is read-only, SIEM configuration and session monitoring are unavailable.
Failback to main region
After the CyberArk SRE team completes the failback to the main region, Audit data synchronization begins. The process can take up to 24 hours. When the DR mode banner disappears, synchronization is complete.
View Audit events that took place during a CRDR incident
In the Audit Activities page, the icon indicates if the event took place during DR mode.
You can view Audit events that occurred in DR mode during a specific time period by creating a report.
For more information about Audit system activities during a CRDR incident, see CRDR Audit events.
Create a report and filter for DR events
-
In the Audit Space, go to System activities > Activities reports , and click Create report.
-
In the Create a report popup, enter the required information and click Apply.
-
Open the downloaded .csv file, locate the Is DR column, and filter for Is DR TRUE.
Resolve missing audit data
Perform one or more of the following actions if you are missing audit data:
-
Check if the DR mode banner still appears indicating that the synchronization is still in process.
-
Confirm that the tenant is back in the main region.
-
Contact your CyberArk administrator if the synchronization exceeds 24 hours.

Unmanaged Privileged Accounts (UPA) detection enables you to detect when a privileged account that is not managed by the CyberArk PAM Vault connects to a target machine. This type of detection can reduce security risks by alerting you about security gaps in your PAM configuration that can potentially be used by malicious actors.
UPA supports detections of unmanaged connections to the following machines:
-
Windows on-premise and Cloud-hosted machine/VM
-
*NIX on-premise and Cloud-hosted machine/VM
ISI integrates with your SIEM system to forward logon data to ISI and then ISI analyzes the logon activity. For more information, see Configure ISI to receive SIEM events.
If an unmanaged privileged account is detected, you can enable a remediation action that adds the account to the CyberArk PAM's Pending Accounts list. The account can then be manually onboarded. We recommend that you enable the automatic remediation option. For more information, see Enable UPA.
Considerations and expected behavior
-
Currently only the Splunk SIEM configuration with heavy forwarders is supported.
-
Unmanaged accounts are considered to be privileged if one of the following scenarios occurs:
-
The accounts were discovered by CyberArk's account discovery tool, are in use, and marked as privileged.
Discovered accounts are listed in the Privilege Cloud Portal's Pending Accounts page.
-
The account's username matches the following pre-defined naming rules:
OS
Account username
Windows
*.admin.*
*NIX
root, admin, ec2-user, ubuntu, centos, fedora
These pre-defined rules are not configurable.
-
-
ISI does not detect or remediate account dependencies.
-
Detected accounts require manual onboarding to CyberArk's PAM Vault regardless of any automatic onboarding rules, if they exist.

You can specify conditions in the key policies and IAM policies that control access to AWS KMS resources. The policy statement is effective only when the conditions are true. For example, you might want a policy statement to take effect only after a specific date. Or, you might want a policy statement to control access only when a specific value appears in an API request.
To specify conditions, you use condition keys in the Condition
element of a policy statement with IAM condition
operators. Some condition keys apply generally to AWS; others are specific to
AWS KMS.
Condition key values must adhere to the character and encoding rules for AWS KMS key policies and IAM policies. For details about key policy document rules, see Key policy format. For details about IAM policy document rules, see IAM name requirements in the IAM User Guide..

Amazon EBS encryption
Use Amazon EBS encryption as a straight-forward encryption solution for your Amazon EBS resources associated with your Amazon EC2 instances. With Amazon EBS encryption, you aren't required to build, maintain, and secure your own key management infrastructure. Amazon EBS encryption uses AWS KMS keys when creating encrypted volumes and snapshots.
Encryption operations occur on the servers that host EC2 instances, ensuring the security of both data-at-rest and data-in-transit between an instance and its attached EBS storage.
You can attach both encrypted and unencrypted volumes to an instance simultaneously. All Amazon EC2 instance types support Amazon EBS encryption.
Contents
Encrypt EBS resources
You encrypt EBS volumes by enabling encryption, either using encryption by default or by enabling encryption when you create a volume that you want to encrypt.
When you encrypt a volume, you can specify the symmetric encryption KMS key to use to encrypt the volume. If you do not specify a KMS key, the KMS key that is used for encryption depends on the encryption state of the source snapshot and its ownership. For more information, see the encryption outcomes table.
Note
If you are using the API or AWS CLI to specify a KMS key, be aware that AWS authenticates the KMS key asynchronously. If you specify a KMS key ID, an alias, or an ARN that is not valid, the action can appear to complete, but it eventually fails.
You cannot change the KMS key that is associated with an existing snapshot or volume. However, you can associate a different KMS key during a snapshot copy operation so that the resulting copied snapshot is encrypted by the new KMS key.
Encrypt an empty volume on creation
When you create a new, empty EBS volume, you can encrypt it by enabling encryption for the specific volume creation operation. If you enabled EBS encryption by default, the volume is automatically encrypted using your default KMS key for EBS encryption. Alternatively, you can specify a different symmetric encryption KMS key for the specific volume creation operation. The volume is encrypted by the time it is first available, so your data is always secured. For detailed procedures, see Create an Amazon EBS volume.
By default, the KMS key that you selected when creating a volume encrypts the snapshots that you make from the volume and the volumes that you restore from those encrypted snapshots. You cannot remove encryption from an encrypted volume or snapshot, which means that a volume restored from an encrypted snapshot, or a copy of an encrypted snapshot, is always encrypted.
Public snapshots of encrypted volumes are not supported, but you can share an encrypted snapshot with specific accounts. For detailed directions, see Share an Amazon EBS snapshot with other AWS accounts.
Encrypt unencrypted resources
You can't directly encrypt existing unencrypted volumes or snapshots.
To encrypt an unencrypted volume, create a snapshot of that volume, and then use the snapshot to create a new encrypted volume. For more information, see Create snapshots and Create a volume.
To encrypt an unencrypted snapshot, create an encrypted copy of that snapshot. For more information, see Copy a snapshot.
If you enable your account for encryption by default, volumes and snapshot copies created from unencrypted snapshots are always encrypted. Otherwise, you must specify the encryption parameters in the request. For more information, see Enable encryption by default.

Data encryption for Amazon Q Business
Amazon Q Business supports encryption at rest using a customer supplied symmetric AWS KMS key when provided, or uses an AWS-owned AWS KMS key if no customer managed key is provided. Amazon Q Business also uses HTTPS protocol for data in transit.
Important
Amazon Q does not support asymmetric KMS keys. For more information, see Using Symmetric and Asymmetric Keys in the AWS Key Management Service Developer Guide.
Encryption at rest
Amazon Q Business provides encryption by default to protect sensitive customer data at rest using AWS owned encryption keys. Sensitive customer data includes both questions and answers in the Amazon Q Business web experience and the documents uploaded to Amazon Q Business index.
The Amazon Q Business uses the questions and answers to know the conversation context and to provide you with the best answer. The conversation data is automatically removed once the conversation is deleted or is inactive. For more information, see Conversation management. The uploaded documents are used by Amazon Q Business to retrieve them at runtime to answer your questions.
-
AWS owned keys – Amazon Q Business uses these keys by default to automatically encrypt sensitive customer data. You can't view, manage, or use AWS owned keys, or audit their use. However, you don't have to take any action or change any programs to protect the keys that encrypt your data. For more information, see AWS owned keys in the AWS Key Management Service Developer Guide.
Encryption of data at rest by default helps reduce the operational overhead and complexity involved in protecting sensitive data. At the same time, it enables you to build secure applications that meet strict encryption compliance and regulatory requirements.
While you can't disable this layer of encryption or select an alternate encryption type, you can add a second layer of encryption over the existing AWS owned encryption keys by choosing a customer managed key when you create your resources:
-
AWS KMS key (KMS) – Amazon Q supports the use of symmetric customer managed keys that you create, own, and manage to add a second layer of encryption over the existing AWS owned encryption.
In Amazon Q Business, you configure KMS keys when you create an Amazon Q Business application environment. The same KMS key is used to encrypt data for the application environment you create and any child resources under the application environment (for example, an Amazon Q Business index). However, KMS keys are not supported for the Amazon Q Business Starter index. So, if you use a KMS key with your application environment, you won't be able to use an Amazon Q Business Starter index for it. To use KMS keys, you must choose either an Amazon Q Business Enterprise index or an Amazon Kendra retriever for your application environment.
Important
Amazon Q does not support asymmetric KMS keys. For more information, see Using Symmetric and Asymmetric Keys in the AWS Key Management Service Developer Guide.
Because you have full control of this layer of encryption, you can perform such tasks as:
-
Establishing and maintaining key policies
-
Establishing and maintaining IAM policies and grants
-
Enabling and disabling key policies
-
Rotating key cryptographic material
-
Adding tags
-
Creating key aliases
-
Scheduling keys for deletion
For more information, see customer managed key in the AWS Key Management Service Developer Guide.
Note
If you have created your Amazon Q Business application environment using AWS KMS and then you want to migrate to using customer managed key (CMK), you will have to re-create your application environment.
Topics
How Amazon Q Business uses grants in AWS KMS
Amazon Q Business requires a grant to use your customer managed key. When you create a Amazon Q Business application environment resource encrypted with a customer managed key, Amazon Q creates a grant on your behalf by sending a CreateGrant request to AWS KMS. Grants in AWS KMS are used to give Amazon Q Business access to a KMS key in a customer account.
Amazon Q Business requires the grant to use your customer managed key for the following internal operations:
-
Send DescribeKey requests to AWS KMS to verify that the symmetric customer managed key ID entered when creating application environment is valid.
-
Send GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlainText requests to AWS KMS to generate data keys encrypted by your customer managed key.
-
Send Decrypt requests to AWS KMS to decrypt the encrypted data keys so that they can be used to encrypt your data.
You can revoke access to the grant, or remove the service's access to the customer managed key at any time. If you do, Amazon Q Business won't be able to access any of the data encrypted by the customer managed key, which affects operations that are dependent on that data.
Create a customer managed key
You can create a symmetric customer managed key by using the AWS Management Console, or the AWS KMS APIs.
Important
Amazon Q does not support asymmetric KMS keys. For more information, see Using Symmetric and Asymmetric Keys in the AWS Key Management Service Developer Guide.
To create a symmetric customer managed key
Follow the steps for Creating symmetric customer managed key in the AWS Key Management Service Developer Guide.
Key policy
Key policies control access to your customer managed key. Every customer managed key must have exactly one key policy, which contains statements that determine who can use the key and how they can use it. When you create your customer managed key, you can specify a key policy. For more information, see Managing access to customer managed keys in the AWS Key Management Service Developer Guide.
To use your customer managed key with your Amazon Q Business resources, the following API operations must be permitted in the key policy:
-
kms:CreateGrant – Adds a grant to a customer managed key. Grants control access to a specified KMS key,which allows access to grant operation Amazon Q Business requires. For more information about Using Grants, see the AWS Key Management Service Developer Guide.
This allows Amazon Q Business to do the following:
-
Call
GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlainText
to generate an encrypted data key and store it, because the data key isn't immediately used to encrypt. -
Call
Decrypt
to use the stored encrypted data key to access encrypted data. -
Set up a retiring principal to allow the service to
RetireGrant
.
-
-
kms:DescribeKey – Provides the customer managed key details to allow Amazon Q to validate the key.
The following are policy statement examples you can add for Amazon Q Business
"Statement": [{ "Sid": "Allow access to principals authorized to use Amazon Q", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/Admin" }, "Action": [ "kms:DescribeKey", "kms:CreateGrant" ], "Resource": "*", "Condition": { "StringEquals": { "kms:ViaService": "qbusiness.region.amazonaws.com", "kms:CallerAccount": "111122223333" } } }, { "Sid": "Allow access for key administrators", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:root" }, "Action": [ "kms:*" ], "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:region:111122223333:key/key_ID" }, { "Sid": "Allow read-only access to key metadata to the account", "Effect": "Allow", "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:root" }, "Action": [ "kms:Describe*", "kms:Get*", "kms:List*", "kms:RevokeGrant" ], "Resource": "*" } ]
For more information about specifying permissions in a policy and troubleshooting key access, see the AWS Key Management Service Developer Guide
Specifying customer managed key for Amazon Q Business
You can specify a customer managed key as a second layer encryption for your Amazon Q Business application environment resource.
When you create your application environment, you can specify the data key by entering a KMS ID, which Amazon Q Business uses to encrypt the identifiable personal data stored by the application environment.
KMS ID – A key identifier for an AWS KMS customer managed key. Enter a key ID, key ARN, alias name, or alias ARN.
Any resources you create under your Amazon Q Business application environment will be encrypted with the same key.
Monitoring your encryption keys for Amazon Q
When you use an AWS KMS customer managed key with your Amazon Q Business resources, you can use AWS CloudTrail or Amazon CloudWatch Logs to track requests that Amazon Q Business sends to AWS KMS.
The following examples are AWS CloudTrail events for CreateGrant
,
GenerateDataKey
, Decrypt
, and DescribeKey
to
monitor KMS operations called by Amazon Q Business to access data encrypted by your
customer managed key.
Encryption in transit
Amazon Q Business uses the HTTPS protocol to communicate with your client application environment. It uses HTTPS and AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) to communicate with other services on your application environment's behalf.

Suspected Credential Theft (SCT) detection
This topic describes Suspected Credential Theft.
Overview
Suspected Credential Theft (SCT) enables you to detect when an account was used to connect to an asset without first retrieving credentials from the CyberArk PAM Vault. This type of detection can alert you to potential credentials theft by an unauthorized user or attacker.
SCT supports detections of unauthorized connections to the following machines:
-
Windows on-premise and Cloud-hosted machine/VM
-
*NIX on-premise and Cloud-hosted machine/VM
ISI integrates with your SIEM system to forward logon data to ISI and then ISI analyzes the logon activity. For more information, see Configure ISI to receive SIEM events.
If suspicious login activity is detected, you receive an SCT alert and can review and investigate it in the ISI Explorer window.
In addition, you can configure ISI to remediate SCT events. If there is an SCT event, ISI automatically triggers a request to the CyberArk PAM Vault to rotate the credentials of the detected account.
For more information, see View and analyze Suspected Credential Theft events.
Considerations and expected behavior
-
Currently only the Splunk SIEM configuration with heavy forwarders is supported.
-
It may take approximately 24 hours for newly onboarded accounts to be assessed by SCT detection. During this period, you will not get SCT alerts on accounts that are already being managed in the CyberArk PAM Vault.
-
SCT detection only supports accounts that are stored in CyberArk's PAM Vault with an address of FQDN or hostname. Accounts stored by IP address are not currently supported.
-
SCT is triggered only when the credentials were not retrieved from CyberArk's PAM Vault within 8 hours prior to when the account connected to the target machine.
-
SCT events do not contain information about the user who leveraged the account that initiated the detected connection.

What is Privileged Detection?
This topic describes Privileged Detection.
Introduction
Currently, many organizations cannot identify high-risk behavior, abuse of privileges, bypassing of privileged account security controls already in place, and any other anomalous activity performed by an organization's users at the earliest stages of the attack lifecycle – before systems are compromised and permanent damage has been done.
Security teams are not able to automate threat detection and risky behavior detection on sensitive systems during user activities. Although investments are made to have proper PAM controls put into place, there is still a lack of ability to detect bypassing attempts by attackers or even internal employees.
With ISI, organizations can now automatically detect and respond to privileged security events.
Privileged Detection types
The following Privileged Detection types are supported in Identity Security Intelligence:
-
Privileged Risky Activity
-
Suspected Credential Theft
-
Unmanaged Privileged Accounts
-
Anomalous Retrieval of Secrets

Manage versions
This topic describes how to use the version history in CyberArk Identity Flows
You can save and manage different versions of a flow as it changes over time, which helps avoid data loss and makes it easier to understand, track, and explore changes over time. If a recent change introduces a problem, you can return to a previous version without rebuilding the flow from the beginning.
You can use the version history to do the following:
- Restore a previous version.
- Track changes over time. Each saved version includes a summary of what was added, removed, or updated, along with the time and author.
- Test different ideas. You can clone any version to explore new logic without affecting the original flow.
- Control what runs in production. You can tag a specific version as the default so only that version is used, even if other changes are in progress.
- Work more efficiently as a team. Versioning makes it easier for multiple users to contribute while keeping a clear record of who made which changes.
- Create clean copies. If you want to reuse a flow's logic for another purpose, you can clone a version into a new flow with no history.
Versioning reduces manual tracking and provides tools to help you maintain reliable and well-documented flows.
Version limits
The version history supports a maximum of 50 versions.
After you have saved the 50th version, you must delete one or more versions before you can save a new version, or clone the flow to continue working.
Save a version
Before you save a flow for the first time, no saved versions exist. After you have saved a flow for the first time, the Version history tab shows one version.
- Select Save > Save as new version.
- In the change note that appears, the note includes information about new or removed nodes and updates to existing nodes.
- Add any information about this version that you might want to refer to in the future, up to 1,000 characters.
- Click Save version.
Clicking Save without creating a new version save changes in the current version.
View version history
- Click Version history in the right panel.
- Browse the timeline to see:
version numbers
the latest and default versions
change logs with timestamp and author
Set a version as the default
You can choose which version of a flow should be used when the flow runs. Setting a version as the default ensures that changes in newer versions do not affect production behavior until you are ready.
To set a version as the default:
- Click Version history.
- Select More actions (...) next to the version you want to set as the default.
- Click Set as default.
The selected version will now be used when the flow runs.
Delete a version
You can remove any version except the default version. You can only delete versions if you have write access.
You cannot restore a deleted version. Make sure the version is not needed before deleting it.
- Click Version history.
- Select More actions (...) next to the version you want to delete.
- Click Delete.
Deleted versions appear in red and are no longer usable.
Clone a version
- Click Version history.
- Select More actions (...) next to the version you want to clone.
- Enter a new flow name, description, and any tags.
- Click OK.
A new flow with no version history is created.

This page shows you how to enable App Check in an iOS app. When you enable App Check, you help ensure that only your app can access Google's OAuth 2.0 endpoints on behalf of your project. See an Overview of this feature.
App Check uses App Attest to help verify that OAuth 2.0 requests are coming from your authentic app. App Check does not use App Attest to analyze fraud risk.
Before you begin
Make sure you have Xcode 12.5 or newer.
Integrate Google Sign-in into your iOS app, using the Google Sign-in library.
1. Set up your project
App Check can be enabled in the Google API Console or in the Firebase Console. It is not necessary to enable it in both places, just one is sufficient.
Google API Console
The following requirements must be met to successfully enable App Check for your iOS client:- You must specify a team ID for your iOS client.
- You must not use a wildcard in your bundle ID since it can resolve to more than one app. This means that the bundle ID must not include the asterisk (*) symbol.
After enabling App Check, you will start seeing metrics related to OAuth requests from your client in the edit view of the OAuth client. Requests from unverified sources won't be blocked until you enforce App Check. The information in the metrics monitoring page can help you determine when to start enforcement.
You might see errors related to the App Check feature when enabling App Check for your iOS app. To fix these errors, try the following:
- Verify that the bundle ID and team ID you specified are valid.
- Verify that you are not using a wildcard for the bundle ID.
Firebase Console
You must have a Firebase project to use App Check with Google Sign-in.
If your app already uses Firebase, use the same project.
If your app uses Google Sign-in, but not Firebase, you already have a Google Cloud project. Add Firebase to your Google Cloud project by selecting it when you create a new project in the Firebase console
See also: Relationship between Firebase projects and Google Cloud
If you haven't already done so, add your iOS apps to your Firebase project using the Project settings page of the Firebase console.
Register your apps to use App Check with the App Attest provider in the App Check section of the Firebase console.
Make sure all of your project's OAuth clients are linked to an app.
If you have unlinked clients, you'll see a message in the Google Identity for iOS section of the App Check page that says, "You have n unlinked OAuth clients which require additional setup."
Additionally, if you have deleted some OAuth clients after setting them up in App Check, you'll see a message that says, "You have n overrides with no matching OAuth client". You can safely clean up by deleting those overrides.
You can link unlinked clients to an existing or new app on the OAuth clients page of the Firebase console.

or higher :SPM

Next steps
Once the App Check library is installed in your app, start distributing the updated app to your users.
The updated client app will begin sending App Check tokens along with every request it makes to Google's authentication endpoints, but the endpoints won't require the tokens to be valid until you enable enforcement in the App Check section of the Firebase console.
Monitor metrics
Before you enable enforcement, however, you should make sure that doing so won't disrupt your existing legitimate users. On the other hand, if you're seeing suspicious use of your app resources, you might want to enable enforcement sooner.
To help make this decision, you can look at App Check metrics for Google Sign-in.
Enable App Check enforcement
When you understand how App Check will affect your users and you're ready to proceed, you can enable App Check enforcement.
Use App Check in debug environments
If, after you have registered your app for App Check, you want to run your app in an environment that App Check would normally not classify as valid, such as a simulator during development, or from a continuous integration (CI) environment, you can create a debug build of your app that uses the App Check debug provider instead of App Attest.

What is Workforce Password Management?
Workforce Password Management (WPM) is a password manager that provides user-friendly methods to store data from business applications in a centralized cloud or vault and securely share it with other users in the organization. For example, this data may include website URLs, usernames, passwords, and notes.
The challenge
Applications that do not implement modern identity protocols and require a username and password pose many challenges for IT security organizations and users, including:
-
Insecure password storage methods. Employees use insecure practices for remembering their passwords, such as writing them down on paper.
-
Poor visibility and control. Without single sign-on (SSO) solutions, accessing websites and productivity tools present a significant risk to IT security teams. You cannot track application access, control password complexity, or revoke access to applications when no longer needed.
-
Increased complexity. Some business applications can only be accessed by multiple people by using the same set of credentials, increasing the complexity of auditing access activity.
-
Inconsistent user experience and password fatigue. Today’s workers conduct business from any place, at any time, using any device. Without centralized password and account management tools, users rely on a patchwork of methods that provide a poor user experience and put your business credentials at a higher risk.
The solution
WPM overcomes the authentication and auditing challenges presented by business applications requiring individual usernames and passwords.
Secure password management
You can store all passwords for business applications in the CyberArk Identity Cloud or optional PAM - Self-Hosted Vault. You decide how accounts and credentials are stored, managed, and retrieved. For example, if you have a PAM - Self-Hosted Vault, you can automatically store all new credentials there and users can retrieve them without connecting to a VPN. In addition, you can require users to pass secondary authentication challenges to sign in to their User Portal. WPM can also secure text-based items such as serial numbers, licenses, PINs, or other secrets in addition to credentials.
Strong controls
WPM provides visibility into user access thus enabling you to enforce stronger controls over password- based credentials. For example, you can use out-of-the-box reporting to see who accessed a specific application or website at a particular time. With the CyberArk Identity Browser Extension, you can also prevent users from saving passwords in the built-in browser password managers, reducing the number of account and credential repositories.
Simplified access to business apps
The Browser Extension automatically recognizes when new passwords are entered, helps generate complex passwords, saves them in the cloud or self-hosted Vault, and adds application shortcuts to users’ individual User Portals. Users simply click on app shortcuts to launch applications, and the Browser Extension opens up sign-in pages and fills out stored credentials. The optional integrations with CyberArk Identity SSO and adaptive multi-factor authentication (MFA) extend one-click access to all types of applications and provide an additional layer of security with context and risk-aware secondary authentication methods.
How it works
Workforce Password Management:
-
Enables the Browser Extension to recognize when credentials are typed in and offers to save them, adding the app to the User Portal. Users can sign in by clicking the app in the User Portal or directly at the application website where the browser will auto-fill the credentials.
-
Integrates with adaptive MFA to provide step-up authentication for specific users and applications, with a wide variety of supported authentication factors including passwordless challenges.
-
Enables you to control which users can view, edit, or share credentials. WPM can automatically transfer ownership with primary owner leaves the organization.
-
Tracks user application access so you can gain visibility by running pre-built reports.
-
Enforces good password hygiene by enabling users to generate unique and strong passwords.
-
Provides users with a means to securely store text- based notes like license keys, PINs, serial numbers, or any other confidential secrets.
User flow
Users click on tiles in the User Portal to complete authentication and open their applications. Password credentials can be stored in the CyberArk Cloud or PAM - Self-Hosted Vault.

Create flows
This topic describes how to create a flow. You can create flows by dragging and dropping the components from the builder to the Identity Flows canvas.
Overview
A flow is made up of components that, when run, performs an ordered set of tasks. Each component performs a specific action within the flow. To add components to a flow, you drag and drop the required components in the Identity Flows builder. For example, you can drag connector components to retrieve data from API endpoints and condition components to define actions to take on the retrieved data.
After you have created a flow, you can be publish it as an app on the CyberArk Identity User Portal. When users open the app, the flow is triggered. Like other apps available in the user portal, access is controlled via CyberArk Identity user and group permissions. Other ways to trigger flows are scheduled flow executions and webhook calls.
A common Identity Flows use case is using the UI to build a flow that interfaces between different services (for example, cloud service providers) and end users. For example, you can create a flow that performs the following actions when a user opens an app:
-
Prompts the user for input via a form component
-
Uses the inputted data to call a cloud service API (for example, Azure)
-
Transforms the API's response data (to make it compatible with a different service provider's APIs)
-
Sends the transformed data to a different service provider (for example, CyberArk Identity)
Trigger flows
You can configure flows to run using any of the following triggers:
-
Running an app in the user portal
-
Running a flow from the builder
-
Defining a webhook which is called by a service or another flow
-
Adding a schedule, which runs the flow at the specified time intervals
-
Manually calling a flow's URL (see Send HTTP flow requests)
Flows builder
You create flows with the builder, which includes these areas and options:
-
Component menu on the left, from where you drag connectors, conditions, and other components
-
Canvas in the center, used to built the flow's logic
-
Configuration options on the right, where flow components are configured (defining authorizations, endpoints, data mappings, and other settings)
-
Top menu above the canvas, with the following options:
-
Save: saves the opened flow
-
Run: runs the opened flow
-
Export: exports the opened flow, which can be imported into other Flows deployments
-
Clone: creates a copy of the opened flow
-
Import: imports a flow (for information on how to map imported flows connector authorizations, see Set imported flow authorizations)
-
Delete: deleted the opened flow
-
-
Notifications icon in the top-right corner, used to view flow logs (see Replay and troubleshoot flows)
Connectors
Connectors define calls to API endpoints. After dragging a connector to the canvas, you can define the endpoint's:
-
URL, method (for example, GET, POST), and content type (such as
application/json
) -
URL parameters and queries
-
Header fields
-
Body payload
In addition to Identity Flows prebuilt connectors for accessing cloud services (such as ServiceNow, Azure, and AWS connectors), where the APIs fields are preconfigured, you can create custom connectors to other REST APIs. For more information on configuring connectors, see Authorize connector API calls
Authorizations
In Identity Flows, you can create and store API authorization and authentication methods, including OAuth2, HMAC, API key, and basic authorization. For OAuth2 authentications, you can also define the scopes required to perform operations when calling the service provider's endpoint. After you have configured an authentication method, you can attach it to a connector (see Authorize a connector). Often, one authorization can be used with multiple endpoints from a single service provider. For example, you can create a Slack authorization with the scopes required to get users and post messages, and then attach the authenticator to both the Post Message and Users List connectors.
For instructions on how to configure and authorize a connector to CyberArk Identity, see the Authorize CyberArk Identity Platform APIs example.
Map flow data
Data defined or retrieved in one component is available in all subsequent components. This enables mapping and transforming data as required from component to component (such as when you want to call an API with data collected from a previous connector). For information about mapping flow data, see Define and map flow data

How K12 schools can transform: Announcing new generative AI maturity readiness assessment
The artificial intelligence (AI) era arrived with a bang—and it’s here to stay. With 60 percent of US students already using generative AI tools, school leaders are trying to get ahead of this trend. They know that while AI has the potential to be transformative for K12 schools, it must be implemented carefully.
Amazon Web Services (AWS) is helping K12 school leaders understand how to leverage this new technology in the most practical and responsible ways. Together with the Council of the Great City Schools and the Consortium for School Networking, we created the K-12 Readiness Checklist and the newly released K12 Generative AI Maturity Readiness Assessment. These are fundamental tools to guide school districts as they implement generative AI in their schools. Following these guidelines, AI can be safely leveraged to assist educators and administrators in both classrooms and school operations. Take the assessment today, and read this post to learn seven ways that AI can transform K12.
- Predict trends and identify patterns—earlier and faster
One key advantage of AI is its ability to analyze large amounts of data quickly. This not only allows humans to identify answers that might have taken weeks or months to detect—if at all—but it also allows them to ask questions that may never have occurred in the first place. For schools, this ability to identify patterns and trends has multiple applications. By drawing on data like school history, birth rates, population growth, and real estate changes, school leaders can predict enrollment patterns, allowing them to plan appropriately. On the classroom level, educators can leverage AI to predict variables contributing to student success, such as attendance and grade data, and compare them with previous years. This data can help pinpoint students who might be starting to struggle, allowing for timely interventions that lead to improvements both in retention and overall academic performance.
- Vastly speed up recordkeeping
Thanks to a type of AI known as intelligent document processing (IDP), schools can free staff from hours of filing and paperwork. When families submit forms, for example, IDP can scan them, file them in the right place, and provide next steps. This can transform recordkeeping tasks in a number of different areas, such as student registration, cumulative folders, and student health records. For student registrations, AI can help student information systems (SIS) handle a complex process that requires managing everything from birth certificates to school transcripts. For student cumulative folders, AI can clean up a process that, to this day, often relies on paper records clogging up storerooms with massive amounts of discipline files, attendance, and progress reports. Lastly, IDP can streamline student health records like immunization information, vision/hearing screenings, and prescriptions administered by nurses.
- Maximize websites and help desks
Another way to reduce the burden on staff is to make it simpler for families and students to find necessary information on their own. Here is where AI-powered chatbots can help. Capable of natural language processing (NLP) and analyzing human speech, chatbots can be leveraged in websites, help desks, or call centers to enhance user experience while improving operational efficiency. Instead of having to spend hours fielding repetitive queries, staff time can be reserved for answering questions the chatbot cannot handle. This same type of AI can also be employed to rapidly sift through documents and video content, such as minutes and notes from staff and board meetings, pulling out relevant information or providing summaries and transcriptions.
- Create custom content
Lesson planning is a time-intensive activity that requires a great deal of content creation. Enter generative AI, which quickly sums up academic resources and uses it to map content. This allows educators to sync the content to learning objectives; adapt it to students with different learning styles or special abilities (such as individualized education plans (IEPs) and 504 plans); create varied, updated, and dynamic teaching materials; or generate a personalized digital tutor that is tailored to specific school curricula. In an era where professional burnout and teacher turnover represent serious challenges, generative AI makes it possible for educators to do what they do best: teach.
- Improve school safety
School safety is a critical issue for school leaders, and something AI can address. K12-centered solutions are being developed that use AI-powered object recognition in videos or images to automatically detect guns, weapons, or fights in school video camera feeds. In addition to enhancing school safety, the technology enables quicker response time to security incidents. AI can also monitor suspicious activity on the web, such as threats, cyberbullying, and suicidal intent, or monitor in-school online behavior patterns to detect potential warning signs before they escalate.
- Automating grading and recordkeeping
Just as AI can free staff from mindless paperwork, it can do the same for teachers. By creating fair criteria, eliminating subjectivity and bias, and providing consistent results based on datasets of previous work, AI can be used to streamline what is often a cumbersome grading process. For writing assignments, it can provide personalized and constructive feedback, giving students the tools they need to improve. AI can also help teachers complete required administrative work such as student cumulative folders and professional development or licensing documentation.
- Deploying chatbots for student practice
While chatbots can be used to resolve queries and pull relevant information from meetings, they have another very practical use: offering students real-time practice with mathematics, foreign languages, and other areas where memorization or flashcard drills have traditionally been used. Using NLP, chatbots can generate flashcards based on individualized needs, drawing from study guides, conceptual maps, or class notes. AI can also repurpose existing PDFs and slide presentations to make flashcards and other materials with the click of a button. All of this allows students to try out new skills in a low-stakes atmosphere, without judgment, while allowing teachers to focus their time on more personalized instruction.
What to do next
The potential for AI in K12 education is enormous—but as with any new technology, it needs to be implemented carefully and responsibly. Issues such as accuracy, fairness, bias, security, and affordability all must be addressed to ensure that AI helps rather than harms. But with more than half of students in the US increasing their use of generative AI tools, this is not a conversation that can be postponed. Take the K12 Generative AI Maturity Readiness Assessment today to identify your generative AI readiness and to pinpoint specific areas that require further attention and investment to ensure safe and secure adoption of this transformative technology.

Identity Flows function reference
This topic lists all available functions that can be called to manipulate flow data.
Overview
When you create a flow, you often need to change the data that is passed from one component to another component. For example, you might need to change the structure of an incoming webhook body request to enable using the data in a connector. To facilitate data manipulation, Flows has inbuilt functions that can be called as needed. For information on how to call functions, see Define and map flow data.

Harden your Workforce Password Management deployment
This topic provides recommendations to harden your users' endpoints and browsers to ensure the controls you implement with Workforce Password Management are not circumvented by a malicious actor.
These recommendations are the minimal requirements for protecting your CyberArk Identity deployment. You must follow the recommendations in this topic or use equivalent methods (based on your organization's relevant expertise) to secure your deployment. Additional security measures may be applied based on your organization's standards.
Enforce secure authentication to CyberArk Identity
Requiring your users to authenticate with from Secure Zones with strong passwords and multi-factor authentication is the first step toward reducing the risks of a breach.
Require strong passwords
Update password requirements to make sure users don't create simple passwords that are easily compromised through techniques such as phishing, social engineering, or brute force attacks.
Refer to NIST Special Publication 800-63B Appendix A for more information about the recommended length and complexity of passwords.
To specify user password requirements
-
Log in to the Identity Administration portal.
-
Click Core Services > Policies.
-
Select the relevant policy set or create a new one.
-
Go to User Security Policies > Password Settings and configure user password requirements and password age as described below:
Password configuration options Option
Description
Minimum password length
You can select the minimum password length required for a password for CyberArk Cloud Directory users. The default is 8.
Maximum password length
You can select the maximum length required for a password for CyberArk Cloud Directory users. The default is 64.
Require at least one digit
You can require at least one digit in the password for CyberArk Cloud Directory users. The default is Yes.
Require at least one uppercase and one lowercase letter
You can require at least one uppercase and one lowercase letter in the password for CyberArk Cloud Directory users. The default is Yes.
Require at least one symbol
You can require at least one symbol in the password for cloud users. The default is No.
Show password complexity for Active Directory users
You can display the password complexity requirements for Active Directory users. The checkbox is unselected by default.
This is an early access feature. Early access features are made available on a case-by-case basis by request. Early access features might see more frequent updates compared to GA features. Contact CyberArk Support to enable this feature.
Show password complexity requirements when entering a new password
You can display the password complexity requirements when updating a user account password. The default is No.
If you select yes, you can enter the requirements in the Password complexity requirements for directory services other than CyberArk Cloud Directory text box.
Limit the number of consecutive repeated characters
The password cannot contain consecutive repeated characters equal to or more than the set value. The default is to allow consecutive repeated characters.
Check against weak password
You can select Yes to check if password contains dictionary or spatial word(s), No to save password without password-strength checking, or "--" to use the default setting, which is No.
Allow username as part of password
You can select Yes to allow the username in the password, No to disallow the username in the password, or "--" to use the default setting, which is Yes.
Allow display name as part of password
You can select Yes to allow part of the display name in the password, No to disallow part of the display name in the password, or "--" to use the default setting, which is Yes.
Require at least one Unicode character
You can require at least one unicode character which is categorized as an alphabetic character but is not uppercase or lowercase.
You can select Yes to require the user to have at least one unicode in the password, No to require no unicode in the password, or "--" to use the default setting, which is No.
Exclude selected words from passwords
You can select Yes to prevent users from including selected words in their passwords, No to allow any words, or “—” to use the default setting, which is No. You can enter the excluded words, separated by a comma and a space, in the Exclude the following word text field. The character maximum is 200.
This is an early access feature. Early access features are made available on a case-by-case basis by request. Early access features might see more frequent updates compared to GA features. Contact CyberArk Support to enable this feature.
Minimum password age before change is allowed
You can require users to enter a minimum password age before a change is allowed. The default is 0 days. Users will not be allowed to change or reset their password until the current password is at least this old.
Maximum password age
You can enter the number of days until the new password expires. The default is 365 days. After the password expires, users are prompted to enter their current password and then enter a new one.
You can use 0 (zero) if you do not want to specify a password expiration period.
Password history
You can set the number of passwords to save by using the drop-down menu to select the number of most recent passwords to save or "--" to use the default setting. The user cannot re-use the passwords on this list. The number you enter is displayed in the message when the user is prompted to enter a new password.
Password Expiration Notification
You can select the number of days before a user's password expires to begin posting a notification of expiration through a portal banner and daily emails. This policy applies to CyberArk Cloud Directory users and Active Directory accounts.
Escalated Password Expiration Notification
You can select the number of hours before a user's password expires to present a change password dialog. The dialog is automatically displayed when the user logs in. This policy applies to CyberArk Cloud Directory users and Active Directory accounts.
This policy is not supported on mobile clients.
Enable password expiration notifications on enrolled mobile devices
When enabled, password expiration notifications are sent to enrolled mobile devices provided Allow Notifications is enabled for the device in the User Portal. The default setting "--" is equivalent to Yes.
Contact Support if password expiration notifications are not set as expected. This feature requires tenant configuration. -
Click Save.
Require multi-factor authentication from a Secure Zone
You can specify which authentication mechanisms users must provide to access the service (authentication profiles), as well as if and when multi-factor authentication is required (authentication rules). For example, you can create a rule to require that users provide a password and text message confirmation code if they are coming from an IP address that is outside of your corporate IP range. To specify this requirement, you need to create a rule and associate it with an authentication profile.
Before you configure MFA for anything, first decide what authentication mechanism you want to use, then make sure your users have that mechanism configured for their user account.
A built-in report is available to view whether users have setup the necessary information for multi-factor authentication challenges. For example, if you plan to use SMS confirmation codes as an authentication factor, you need to make sure all users impacted by the authentication policy have a mobile number associated with their account, otherwise they might be locked out.
Additional licenses might be required for access to all authentication mechanisms. Contact CyberArk Support for more information.

Configure settings to transfer application credential ownership
If an application owner is deprovisioned from CyberArk Identity, application access is removed for all recipients that share the application. To allow recipients of the shared application to continue using the application, you can transfer application credential ownership to another user in the event that the original owner is deprovisioned from CyberArk Identity.
To configure settings to transfer application credential ownership
-
In the Identity Administration portal select Core Services > Policies > User Security Policies > User Account Settings > User Shared Apps.
-
Click the checkbox next to Transfer ownership of shared app credentials.
-
Select the Owner type (Manager or Specified User) and click Add to enter a priority list to transfer ownership.
Credential ownership is transferred in the order specified in the Owner List and one at a time. For example, if the owner list includes two names, ownership is transferred to the first name or Manager in the list. If the first person is not available in CyberArk Identity, then next person in the list is used and so on.
Owner Type Description Manager Transfers ownership of the shared application to the manager specified in the Users > Account page (for the original application owner). If no manager is specified in the Users > Account page and the original owner is deprovisioned from CyberArk Identity, the shared application is no longer available to recipients of the shared application. Specified User Transfers ownership of the shared application to the user(s) you select. If you want the new owner to have the ability to share the application with new recipients, make sure they are in a Role with the Shared Credentials Administrative Right; otherwise the new owner can't share the application credentials with new recipients. -
Click Save.
Harden endpoints
Removing administrator privileges for end users is a critical step toward preventing security breaches. Refer to CyberArk Endpoint Privilege Manager documentation for details about how we can help limit or remove administrator privileges.
Harden browsers
We recommend the following steps to harden endpoints in your environment.
Step 1: Ensure that your environment does not allow unapproved HTTPS proxy, sniffer, or similar software.
Attackers can use phishing and social engineering to trick users into downloading their malicious HTTPS proxy, sniffer, or similar software. If a user installs malicious software, it provides attackers with access to all internet traffic.
Step 2: Manage browsers in your organization.

-
The ability to disable the less secure, built-in password managers that might conflict with the CyberArk Identity Browser Extension
